titre: Keshan Disease Came From the Soil, Not the Plate
accroche: In 1935, a deadly cardiomyopathy strikes isolated Chinese villages. The cause lies in the soil their wheat grows in.
contenu_vulgarise:
In the winter of 1935, in Keshan County in northeastern China, local doctors begin recording sudden deaths among children and young women in isolated farming villages. The heart fails within days, sometimes within hours, with no apparent infection. The disease takes the name of the county where it was described. It strikes almost exclusively households that live off their own grain harvest: according to a 2021 review, 99% of these families' food comes from their own fields, and 80% of patients are young women of childbearing age or infants recently weaned.

## A Trace Element Missing From the Soil, Not the Plate

Over the following decades, epidemiological surveys map out the disease: a wide band running from northeastern to southwestern China, which lines up almost exactly with the regions where the soil is poor in selenium. This trace element, needed in minute amounts by an enzyme that protects heart cells, passes from the soil to the plant, then to whoever eats it. A household that diversifies its diet with food from elsewhere makes up for poor soil; a household living off its own harvest alone makes up for nothing. Between 1974 and 1977, a team from the Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences tests the hypothesis in the field, in Mianning County, Sichuan. Children aged 1 to 9 receive, half of them, a weekly tablet of sodium selenite, and the other half a placebo. In 1974, 13.5% of children in the control group fall ill, against 2.2% in the treated group. In 1975: 9.5% against 1.0%. Faced with such a gap, the team stops withholding treatment from half the children: in 1976, all receive selenite, and the incidence drops to 0.32%; in 1977, to zero.

## The Shift

One could conclude that Keshan disease is purely a deficiency, and stop there. The researchers who studied it don't: selenium explains why some regions are affected and others aren't, but not entirely why the disease strikes in waves, worse in some years than others, in the same villages. Part of the answer is viral: a mutated strain of an otherwise ordinary virus, coxsackievirus B3, appears to turn more aggressive specifically in selenium-deficient bodies, which lose part of their antioxidant defense against it. For a long time, a disease had to be filed as either infectious or dietary, as if one had to rule out the other: Keshan disease shows a deficiency that opens the door to an infection, and an infection that might not be as severe without the deficiency. The soil and the virus don't exclude each other: they follow one another.

repere.texte: Among children aged 1 to 9 in Mianning County (Sichuan), the incidence of Keshan disease drops from 13.5% (control group) to 2.2% (sodium selenite group) in 1974, then from 9.5% to 1.0% in 1975. In 1976 and 1977, with all children now treated, it falls to 0.32%, then to 0%.
repere.source: Keshan Disease Research Group, Chinese Medical Journal, 1979, 92(7):471-476; figures reproduced and confirmed by Vinceti et al., Molecular Medicine Reports, 2017

carte.punch: A child's heart fails, because of soil too poor in selenium.
carte.idee: In isolated Chinese villages living off their own harvest, a trace element in the soil, selenium, is missing from the plate. Between 1974 and 1977, giving children sodium selenite made the incidence of a deadly cardiomyopathy drop from 13.5% to 2.2%, then to zero.

quiz.question: Why did Keshan disease strike some Chinese villages for so long and not others, with otherwise similar diets?
choix: Because these villages ate only dried meat, with no fresh vegetables at all
Because their wheat grew in soil poor in selenium, with no other food source to make up for it
Because they drank well water contaminated by a local heavy metal
Because they observed a prolonged religious fast every winter
quiz.explication: The disease tracks the selenium content of the soil, a trace element plants absorb and pass on to whoever eats them. The affected villages lived almost entirely off their own harvest, with no outside food to compensate. No source documents an exclusively meat-based diet, metal contamination, or a religious fast as the cause here.
